content: Bananadine is a fictional psychoactive substance that was falsely claimed to be extractable from banana peels. The original recipe for extracting this substance was published as a hoax in the Berkeley Barb in March 1967. This hoax gained further attention when William Powell, believing the claim to be true, included the method in The Anarchist Cookbook in 1970, referring to it as Musa Sapientum Bananadine, a name derived from the banana's scientific classification. However, scientific research conducted at New York University has confirmed that banana peels do not contain any intoxicating chemicals. Smoking banana peels produces no psychoactive effects and only results in a placebo effect. Banana peels do contain significant amounts of the non-psychoactive neurotransmitters tyramine and dopamine. These compounds can have physiological effects, particularly in individuals taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs). Dopamine, while present, does not produce psychoactive effects when derived from banana peels. Bananas also contain tryptophan, an amino acid that is metabolized into serotonin in the body. Increased serotonin levels can have mood-enhancing effects, including a reduction in symptoms of depression, as demonstrated in studies by Leathwood and Pollet (1982) and Sainio et al. (1996). Xiao et al. (1998) found that consuming two bananas daily for three consecutive days increased blood serotonin levels by 16%. However, there is no evidence in the scientific literature to suggest that tryptophan has hallucinogenic properties. On the contrary, tryptophan has been used therapeutically to reduce hallucinations in patients with mental health disorders. Furthermore, the efficacy of smoking tryptophan as a method of administration is highly questionable. The myth of bananadine has persisted in popular culture. Donovan's hit single Mellow Yellow, released in the same month as the Berkeley Barb hoax, was mistakenly believed to be the origin of the myth. However, in a 2005 interview on NPR's Fresh Air, Donovan clarified that the rumor was actually started by folk singer Country Joe McDonald in San Francisco, one week before the release of Mellow Yellow. McDonald has corroborated this account, even recounting how the rumor led to a temporary banana shortage in Berkeley as concert-goers purchased bananas for experimentation. The myth resurfaced in the late 1980s when the satirical punk band The Dead Milkmen released a song referencing the supposed effects of smoking banana peels. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) even investigated the claims at one point. In the liner notes of Experience, the debut album by British electronic group The Prodigy, band member Leeroy Thornhill humorously referenced the myth, inviting people to smoke some banana skins anytime. Additionally, the Ray Stevens song Thirty-Five Year Old Hippie Class Reunion humorously alludes to the hoax, with characters joking about smoking increasingly absurd items, culminating in the suggestion of smoking the contents of an entire pet store.
